title: BEARD v. THE UNITED KINGDOM
summary:
In the case of Beard v. the United Kingdom, the applicants, Mr. and Mrs. Beard, are British citizens who identify as Gypsies by birth, falling within the Council of Europe’s definition of Roma and Travellers. Their case against the United Kingdom centred on their struggle to maintain their traditional way of life—living in caravans—on land they owned in Lancashire. The harm at the heart of the case was the applicants’ inability to lawfully reside in their caravans on their own land, facing repeated refusals of planning permission, enforcement notices, and criminal prosecution, despite their efforts to comply with regulations and their lack of viable alternatives due to safety concerns on official sites.

Chronologically, the Beards purchased a plot of land in 1986, cleaned it up, and applied for planning permission in 1991 to establish a small family caravan site. Their application was refused on grounds of visual amenity and highway safety, and subsequent appeals were dismissed. Enforcement notices required them to vacate the land, and they faced prosecution for unlawful occupation. Attempts to find alternative sites failed, as the only available official site was unsafe due to previous violent attacks against them.

The European Commission of Human Rights examined the case under Article 8 (right to respect for private and family life and home) and Article 14 (prohibition of discrimination) of the European Convention on Human Rights, declaring the application admissible but not finding a violation at this stage. No remedies were awarded.

This case is significant as it highlights the persistent barriers Roma and Traveller families face in securing lawful accommodation that respects their traditional lifestyle, reflecting broader historical patterns of exclusion and the ongoing tension between planning regulations and minority rights in Europe.
